The United States abandoned the gold standard for its currency in March and April 1933 [1], [3], in a series of laws and executive orders, and the government suspended the gold standard for United States currency [4]. [2] mentions the suspension of the convertibility of the U.S. dollar to gold happened in 1971, but that event marked the end of the international gold standard and not the U.S. gold standard specifically.

The Svalbard Global Seed Vault was built in 2008 [1][2][3], specifically on February 26, 2008, although the first seeds arrived in January [2]. The preservation of seeds in the vault is free for end users, with the Norwegian government and the Crop Trust covering operational costs [4].

The national anthem of Trinidad and Tobago is "Forged from the Love of Liberty," written by Patrick S. Castagne [1][3][4][5]. Castagne was a renowned West Indian songwriter who wrote "A Song for Federation" for the West Indies Federation, which was briefly established in 1958 [2][3]. "Forged from the Love of Liberty" was edited and adopted by Trinidad and Tobago after it became independent in 1962 [1][3].

The famous street in New Orleans is Bourbon Street [1], which is known for its numerous bars and strip clubs and is a major tourist attraction in the French Quarter. Other famous streets in New Orleans include St. Charles Avenue [2], which is known for its mansions and tree-lined boulevard, and Frenchmen Street [4], which is home to many live music venues. Royal Street [3] is also located in the French Quarter and is known for its antique shops, art galleries, and hotels.

The song "Do You Want to Know a Secret" was primarily composed by John Lennon but credited to Lennon–McCartney [1, 2]. George Harrison sang the song on the Beatles' album "Please Please Me" [1, 2, 3]. The song reached number 2 on the Billboard chart in the United States as a single by Vee-Jay [1, 3]. Billy J. Kramer also covered the song [3, 4].

The 13th Amendment to the United States Constitution, which abolished slavery and involuntary servitude, was ratified by the required number of states on December 6, 1865 [2][3][4]. The amendment was passed in Congress on April 8, 1864 by the Senate and on January 31, 1865 by the House [2]. Secretary of State Seward proclaimed its adoption on December 18, 1865 [2].

The song "Don't Matter to Me" by Drake featuring posthumous vocals from Michael Jackson was released as the fourth single from Drake's fifth studio album "Scorpion" on July 6, 2018 [1]. Its release date was originally set for July 10, 2018, but was canceled in the United States [1]. The song debuted at number 20 on the "Billboard" Hot 100, but later peaked at number 12 [1]. This was the 31st top-ten song for Drake and the 30th top ten on the chart for Michael Jackson [1, 2]. The song "Doesn't Really Matter" was Michael Jackson's ninth number one on the "Billboard" Hot 100, and received a gold certification in the United States [3]. This song was also considered to influence music videos from several artists [4].

England won the World Cup in soccer in 1966 during the FIFA World Cup that was held in England from 11 to 30 July 1966 [1][2][3][4]. England beat West Germany 4–2 in the final, winning the Jules Rimet Trophy [1]. This was England's only FIFA World Cup title [1][5].

Washington addressed both black and white audiences in his Atlanta Exposition Speech [1][2][3][4][5]. In the speech, he called on the black community to join the world of work and emphasized the opportunities available in the South, particularly in commerce and industry [2]. He also emphasized the importance of education for the black community, but advocated for work and submission to white political rule, in what became known as the Atlanta compromise [3][4].

Alabama adopted a right-to-work law in 1954 during the legislative session, but the law was repealed in 1956 [1]. The right-to-work law was reinstituted in Alabama in 1975, with Edward J. Steimel, the founding executive director of the Louisiana Association of Business and Industry, leading the push for its passage [3, 4]. The Louisiana State Legislature passed a right-to-work law in 1952 [5], but the law was repealed in 1956 [1]. Right-to-work was reinstituted in Louisiana in 1976 [2]. Oklahoma adopted a right-to-work law in 2001 [1].

The first North American Indigenous Games were held in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada in 1990 [1]. These multi-sport events, governed by the North American Indigenous Games Council, aim to bring together indigenous North American athletes while fostering new friendships and cultural events [2]. The games have been held in several locations in Canada and the United States since 1990, including Toronto, Ontario, Canada in 2017 [3].

Stephen King's Dark Tower series consists of eight books: "The Gunslinger", "The Dark Tower", "The Waste Lands", "Wizard and Glass", "Wraiths and Earl Cambion", "The Wind Through the Keyhole", "Song of Susannah", and "The Dark Tower". [1][2][3][4] A ninth book, "The Wind Through the Keyhole", was published in 2012 and serves as a coda to the series. [3]

The Myrtle Beach SkyWheel Ferris wheel is located in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, next to Plyler Park. It opened on May 20th, 2011 and at the time was the tallest Ferris wheel in the United States east of the Mississippi River [1][4]. It was designed and manufactured by Ronald Bussink Professional Rides and Chance Morgan, with glass-enclosed gondolas that each seat six passengers and operate year-round [1]. The wheel's height was chosen to make it an iconic feature for the city and is similar in design to the Niagara SkyWheel on Canada's side of Niagara Falls [1][4]. St. Louis-based developer Koch Development Company chose Myrtle Beach for its new boardwalk, which has its northern end near the site of the SkyWheel [2]. The construction of the building started in December, while the wheel's frame began work in February [4].

Rick and Morty season 3 was originally aired on Cartoon Network's late night programming block Adult Swim, airing on Sundays at 11:30 p.m EST [1][2]. The third season of the series premiered on April 1, 2017, and concluded on October 1, 2017 with a total of ten episodes [1][3].

The term referring to linking a currency value to the value of gold is known as the gold standard [1][2][3]. Under the gold standard, a country's government declares that it will exchange its currency for a certain weight in gold [2]. The gold standard assumes that there are no restrictions on capital movements or export of gold by private citizens across countries [2]. This "rule of exchange" allows anyone to enter the central bank and exchange coins or currency for pure gold or vice versa [2]. The gold standard is a special case of a currency board where the value of the national currency is linked to the value of gold instead of a foreign currency [4].

The first introduction of soccer, also known as football, in the Olympics was at the 1908 Summer Olympics, which was held in London, England [5]. Prior to this, soccer was played at the 1900 and 1904 Summer Olympics, as well as at the 1906 Intercalated Games, but these were not official FIFA-supervised Olympic competitions [5]. The soccer tournament at the Olympics was for amateur players only [4, 5]. The first Olympic soccer tournament to allow professional players was in 1984 [1, 2, 3].

The Cleveland Browns returned to the NFL in 1999, after a three-year period of deactivation [1][4]. This return was facilitated by the return of some of the franchise's assets, including its name, logos, training facility, and history [5]. The franchise was considered a continuation of the previous franchise, as the history and colors of the team remained in Cleveland [3].
St. Petersburg is located in Pinellas County, Florida [1][3]. It is the largest city within the county, and the second-largest in the Tampa Bay Area [1].

The first hand-held camera, in the sense of a device meant to be carried and used like a handheld film camera, was demonstrated by Polish inventor Kazimierz Prószyński in 1898 [1]. However, practical hand-held cameras suitable for filmmaking became available for pioneering filmmakers in the 1890s with the Cinematograph developed by the Lumière brothers [1]. The first handheld amateur camera, marketed to the public, was the Kodak camera introduced by George Eastman in 1888 [3]. Notably, handheld electronic cameras appeared in 1981 with the demonstration of the Sony Mavica [2].

Anne Hathaway portrays the White Queen (Mirana of Marmoreal) in Tim Burton's 2010 adaptation of "Alice in Wonderland" and its sequel "Through the Looking-Glass" [1][2]. In this film adaptation, the White Queen is a punk-rock vegan pacifist, with a delicate exterior that hides her sadistic nature [3]. The White Queen's soldiers in the film are depicted in white armor inspired by chess pieces [1].

The South Carolina Ordinance of Secession was written by various delegates during a convention held in Charleston on December 17, 1860, after a call for secession by William Henry Gist [2]. While several figures played a role in the convention, notably Francis Wilkinson Pickens [3], it was ultimately Christopher Memminger who wrote the "Declaration of the Immediate Causes Which Induce and Justify the Secession of South Carolina from the Federal Union," which was the official document outlining the reasons for secession [1].

This estimate only included direct capital costs, such as the construction of competition venues, the Olympic village, and the media center. Indirect capital costs for infrastructure and other preparations not directly related to staging the Games were not included in the estimate.

The festival of Holi marks the end of winter and the beginning of spring [1][2][3][4][5]. It is a time for enjoying the new season, renewing relationships, and celebrating the arrival of spring [1][2][3]. It is also a thanksgiving for a good harvest [2]. The festival lasts for several days, with activities such as throwing colored water and powders, lighting bonfires, and gathering with friends and family [1][2][3][4]. Holi is observed in many parts of the Indian subcontinent, as well as among members of the diaspora from the Indian subcontinent in other parts of the world [2][4].

The Gadsden Purchase is a region of present-day southern Arizona and southwestern New Mexico that the United States bought from Mexico [1, 2, 4]. The treaty took effect on June 8, 1854, but the first draft was signed on December 30, 1853, by James Gadsden, U.S. ambassador to Mexico, and by Antonio López de Santa Anna, president of Mexico [1, 4]. The purchase covered about 30,000 square miles of Mexico's northern territories for a cost of $10 million [4]. The goal was to build a rail line through southern Arizona to California [2].

The Royal Flying Doctor Service (RFDS) was established on May 15, 1928 in Cloncurry, Queensland [1][3][4]. This service, later known as the RFDS, was formed by Reverend John Flynn, who was inspired to connect doctors and patients in remote locations through the use of radios and aircraft [1][2]. The first aircraft operated by the Aerial Medical Service, the forerunner of the RFDS, was a de Havilland DH.50 hired from the fledgling Queensland and Northern Territory Aerial Service (Qantas) [3][4].

Christina Aguilera's hit single "Genie in a Bottle" was released on June 22, 1999 [1]. The song gained immense popularity, reaching number one on the Billboard Hot 100 and staying there for five consecutive weeks [2]. The success of "Genie in a Bottle" marked the third time that year that a new female artist reached number one on the Hot 100 with her debut single, following Britney Spears and Jennifer Lopez [3]. The single was also a commercial success, selling over 1.3 million copies in the US, making it the second best-selling single of 1999 [4].

The Romans in Britain were ultimately driven out by local warlords and Romano-British themselves, who expelled Roman officials around 410 AD. Some believe that this decision was made after the Romano-British appealed for aid to the Roman Emperor Honorius, and received no response, while others argue that the Britons first took charge of their own affairs and later expelled the Roman officials. The torch for the 2012 Olympics was lit by a team of seven young athletes, each nominated by a famous British Olympian, led by Sir Steve Redgrave [1][2][3][4]. The torch relay also included celebrities and athletes from various countries and fields, such as Matt Smith, Patrick Stewart, Jamie Oliver, and James McAvoy [1][3]. The torch relay included numerous stops throughout the UK, including visits to national heritage sites, key sporting events, and schools [3]. The relay culminated at the London Olympics opening ceremony, where the torch was passed to the young athletes, who then each lit a petal of the Olympic cauldron [1][2].

The Latin term "camera obscura" means "dark room" and refers to a natural optical phenomenon that occurs when a scene at the other side of a screen is projected through a small hole in that screen and forms an inverted image on a surface opposite to the opening [1][2][3][4]. It is not to be confused with the "camera lucida", a light drawing aid that does not project an image [5].

Cricket was introduced to India by British East India Company mariners in the first half of the 19th century [3]. The Oriental Cricket Club, established by the Parsi community in Mumbai (formerly Bombay) in 1848, marks one of the earliest instances of Indians playing the sport [4]. It is believed that the Parsis, being in close contact with the Imperial British, were the first to start cricket in India [4]. An older reference dates the first recorded game of cricket in India to 1721, when British sailors of the East India Company were playing the sport at Cambay, near Baroda [3]. Overall, cricket's arrival in India can be traced back to the East India Company and its influence on Indian territory.

Most of the Earth's crust, about 64.7% by volume, is composed of igneous rocks, the most common of which are basalts and gabbros [1]. The Earth's crust can be divided into the oceanic crust and the continental crust, with oceanic crust being composed primarily of dense (mafic) iron magnesium silicate igneous rocks, like basalt, while the continental crust is less dense, composed of (felsic) sodium potassium aluminium silicate rocks, like granite [2].

An example of a normal measured value for a resting, healthy adult human is 120 mmHg systolic and 80 mmHg diastolic (written as 120/80 mmHg) [1]. The systolic pressure can be obtained with a sphygmomanometer or by palpating the pulse [2].

The term NAT (Network Address Translation) in networking refers to a method of remapping one IP address space into another by modifying network address information in the IP header of packets while they are in transit across a traffic routing device [1][2][3]. This technique is useful for conserving global address space in the face of IPv4 address exhaustion [1][2][3]. One Internet-routable IP address of a NAT gateway can be used for an entire private network [1][2]. Often referred to as IP masquerading, NAT hides an entire IP address space, usually consisting of private IP addresses, behind a single IP address in another, usually public address space [3].

In some regions, the term "rib eye steak" is used for a rib steak without the bone [1]. In other areas, "ribeye" refers to the same cut with the bone in [3].

In soccer, a player can be substituted during a stoppage in play with the permission of the referee [3][4][5]. The player to be substituted must have left the field of play before the substitute may enter the field of play [3]. The incoming player may only enter the field at the halfway line [3]. The maximum number of substitutions permitted in most competitive international and domestic league games is three in 90 minutes, with each team being allowed one more if the game should go into extra-time [5]. Unlimited substitutions are allowed in some sports such as ice hockey [2].

The ratio of the wave height to its wave length is called the significant wave height [1][2][3] [4][5]. It is defined as the mean wave height (trough to crest) of the highest third of the waves, and is calculated as four times the standard deviation of the surface elevation or four times the square root of the zeroth-order moment (area) of the wave spectrum [1][2][3]. The significant wave height is an important parameter for the statistical distribution of ocean waves [1].

The ragtime style of music, which descended from the jigs and march music played by African American bands, started to become popular in the United States in the 1890s and continued to gain widespread popularity throughout the latter part of the 19th century [1][2][3][4]. It was a distinctly American musical style that may be considered a synthesis of African syncopation and European classical music [3]. Despite initial denigration by conservatives and the classically trained establishment, the style continued to flourish and was widely popular by the start of the 20th century [1][3].

The oldest person in the world, according to the Gerontology Research Group and Guinness World Records, was Jeanne Calment from France, who lived to the age of 122 years, 164 days [1][2]. After her death, Susannah Mushatt Jones of the United States became the oldest living person in the world [3]. Emma Morano, another supercentenarian from Italy, later became the world's oldest living person and the last living person who was born in the 1800s following Jones' death in 2016 [4].

The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, which ended the Mexican-American War, was signed on February 2, 1848, in Villa de Guadalupe Hidalgo (now a neighborhood of Mexico City) [1][3]. The treaty was ratified by the U.S. Senate on March 10, 1848 and by Mexico's legislature on May 19, 1848 [5]. The treaty recognized the Rio Grande as the southern boundary of Texas and ceded what is now the states of California, Nevada, Utah, Colorado, Arizona, and New Mexico to the United States [4].

The botanical name of lady finger is Caladenia catenata [1][2][3]. This plant, also known as white caladenia, white fingers, and lady's fingers, is native to New South Wales, Queensland, and Victoria and is a member of the orchid family. Lady finger is a ground orchid with a single hairy leaf and one or two white, sometimes pink flowers.

The downfall of the Inca Empire was primarily due to the Spanish conquest, which began in the 16th century [1][2][3]. The Spanish introduction of Old World diseases, such as smallpox and influenza, to the indigenous population led to rapid population decline and loss of life [1][2]. The Spanish also exploited the Inca labor system, subjecting the indigenous population to hard labor in the gold and silver mines [1]. The Inca resistance to the Spanish was eventually suppressed by 1572 [1][4]. However, some scholars argue that the Inca Empire may have already been in decline before the arrival of the Spanish [5].

Tornadoes are more common in the United States than in any other country, occurring more than 1,200 times annually [1]. Most tornadoes occur east of the Rocky Mountains in the Great Plains, the Midwest, the Mississippi Valley, and the southern United States, which is known as "Tornado Alley." Tornadoes have been reported in every U.S state, with Oklahoma and Kansas being particularly prone to tornado activity [2][3]. Florida, while not having a high number of tornadoes in total, has the most tornadoes per unit area [3][4]. Texas and Southern California also have a significant number of tornadoes [4].
